references.text: Matthew's parallel parable of the sower: what fell among thorns is the one who hears the word, but the cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.

Mark's parallel parable of the sower: those who were sown among thorns hear the word, but the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things choke the word so that it becomes unfruitful.

Paul warns that those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a trap, and many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.
Jesus says that one should not worry about life, what to eat or drink, or about the body. This illustrates how worries for this life can choke spiritual growth.
The parable of the rich farmer who stored up treasures for himself but was not rich toward God. It illustrates how wealth and pleasures in life can become a spiritual trap that chokes faith.

Jesus warns his disciples that their hearts must not be weighed down with carousing, drunkenness, and the worries of this life, so that the day comes upon them unexpectedly. A direct parallel to the theme of worries and pleasures hindering spiritual growth.
Demas left Paul because he loved the present world. A concrete example of how worldly desires and pleasures can choke faith.
John warns against loving the world or the things in the world: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. These correspond to the pleasures and wealth that choke the word.
The image of soil that drinks the rain but bears thorns and thistles, and is near to being cursed. A parallel to the seed that falls among thorns and bears no fruit.
Jeremiah urges Judah to break up new ground and not sow among thorns—an Old Testament image that underlies Jesus' parable of the sower among thorns.
